strings.name: Kyriakos Mitsotakis
strings.role: Prime Minister of Greece and President of New Democracy
strings.summary: Kyriakos Mitsotakis entered parliament after a career in finance and consulting, led New Democracy from 2016, first became prime minister in 2019 and formed another government in 2023. He pursued tax cuts, digital government and same-sex civil marriage reform, while his government faced pressure over living costs, surveillance and accountability for the rail disaster.
strings.coverageNote: Checked through 18 November 2026. Recent activity is supported by an actual interview published by the prime minister’s office on 14 November, without assuming that was the recording date. The 2023 caretaker-government interruption is preserved. Policies, judicial proceedings and personal responsibility are distinguished; future elections and policy goals are not treated as accomplished.
strings.influence.rationale: Leading Greece’s New Democracy and serving as prime minister, he has regional influence on economic recovery, public governance and European cooperation.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and higher education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Athens on 4 March 1968, he earned a Harvard bachelor’s degree in Social Studies in 1990, a Stanford MA in International Relations in 1993 and a Harvard Business School MBA in 1995, according to Parliament’s biography. Social Studies is not silently relabelled sociology, and academic distinctions are separate from degrees.
strings.facts.f2.label: From finance to public affairs
strings.facts.f2.value: Before politics he worked at Chase Investment Bank, McKinsey, Alpha Ventures and the National Bank of Greece group, including about three years as CEO of NBG Venture Capital. Leading the venture-capital subsidiary did not mean being CEO of the entire banking group. The World Economic Forum named him a Global Leader for Tomorrow in 2003.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Economic reform and household pressures
strings.highlights.h1.text: He made tax cuts, investment and digital public services priorities. His office describes the expansion of gov.gr, while his 2026 interview emphasizes growth and debt improvements but acknowledges prices eroding wage gains. Government accounts are not a substitute for independent evaluation of results.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Security governance and judicial accountability
strings.highlights.h2.text: The 2023 Tempi rail disaster killed 57 people, and a trial of 36 defendants opened in March 2026. Separately, four businesspeople were convicted in the spyware case in February 2026, with sentences suspended pending appeal at the time of reporting. The rail case, commercial-spyware convictions and criticism of government oversight are distinct; none establishes a personal conviction of Mitsotakis.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Interview discusses the economy and living costs
strings.timeline.t1.text: His office published the text of his interview with Wall Street Journal journalist Gordon Fairclough, covering debt, investment, wages and price pressures. It confirms an actual interview and his current office. Growth and tax-cut results are presented as his account, while future policy intentions are not reported as fulfilled.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Parliament approves same-sex civil marriage bill
strings.timeline.t2.text: His government’s bill won support from 176 members of the 300-seat parliament, allowing same-sex marriage and adoption. Some governing-party lawmakers opposed it or abstained, with opposition support securing passage. This was the parliamentary vote, not the gazette-publication date, and the reform did not open all assisted-reproduction and surrogacy options.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Sworn in again to lead a majority government
strings.timeline.t3.text: He took the oath after the 25 June election gave New Democracy 158 of 300 seats. May’s first election had not produced a majority government, and Sarmas became caretaker prime minister on 25 May. His tenure since 2019 was therefore not uninterrupted; the two elections also used different seat-allocation rules.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Responds to surveillance of an opposition leader
strings.timeline.t4.text: He acknowledged that the national intelligence service had tapped Androulakis’s phone, denied prior knowledge and called the operation procedurally lawful but politically unacceptable. Legality and lack of knowledge were his claims. Traditional wiretapping and the Predator spyware investigation must not be treated as the same operation without evidence.
strings.timeline.t5.title: First sworn in as prime minister
strings.timeline.t5.text: He succeeded Tsipras after New Democracy won the previous day’s election with 158 of 300 parliamentary seats. Investment, jobs and tax cuts were central promises. Electoral victory, taking the oath and delivering policies are separate stages.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Elected President of New Democracy
strings.timeline.t6.text: He became leader of the then-opposition New Democracy and parliamentary opposition leader. An internal party election was neither appointment as prime minister nor a direct nationwide election of the country’s leader; his first premiership began in 2019.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Becomes administrative reform and e-government minister
strings.timeline.t7.text: He took responsibility for public-administration reform in the Samaras government, serving until 27 January 2015. This ministry is recorded separately from his later party leadership and premiership. Official assessments of reform success do not replace independent audits.
strings.timeline.t8.title: First elected to the Greek parliament
strings.timeline.t8.text: He entered parliament for New Democracy, initially representing Athens B. His office dates entry into public political life to late 2003, while Parliament’s biography confirms first election in March 2004. Beginning political activity and winning election are separate dates.
